attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction, listed under 'High confidence' in his 2025 predictions post.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will continue', filed under high confidence and tied to the end of 2025. The normalised wording keeps the scope: US, consumer protection, generative AI risks.

contract.note: The plain reading (no broad, binding consumer regime for generative AI in force during 2025; narrow laws allowed) is how an ordinary reader would take 'very little'. It leans neither for nor against him. The 'very little' threshold is still an interpretation.

evidence.note: Dated White House fact sheet on the December 2025 order. Its own account of federal action against state AI laws shows a deregulatory federal stance.
Law-firm analysis from about March 2026, before the cutoff. It says no comprehensive federal AI law was enacted and the only major federal AI law is narrow.
The Take It Down Act is a narrow federal statute on deepfake intimate images. Under the contract, a narrow law does not meet the contradiction condition.
California SB 243 was signed in October 2025. It covers one state and one product type, so it is piecemeal, not a widely applicable regime.

reviews.rationale: The end-2025 deadline has passed. No comprehensive federal law was enacted, and federal policy was light-touch and moved to challenge state laws. The counterexamples are narrow: one federal deepfake statute and one state chatbot law. They do not amount to a broad consumer-protection regime, so the support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement, made while reviewing his 2024 predictions.

semantics.note: A present-tense description of the LLM market as of late 2024. The normalised wording matches it.

contract.note: Reading 'moat' as no lasting performance lead and 'price war' as repeated competitive price cuts is ordinary. Setting the period to 2024 fits a post that reviews 2024.

evidence.note: Independent AI Index measurement: the gap between the top two models shrank to 0.7% in 2024, with high-quality models from more developers.
May 2024 reporting of ByteDance, Alibaba, Baidu and iFlytek cutting LLM prices in response to each other. It covers China only, but the claim names no region.

reviews.rationale: Independent data show frontier models from different developers converging in 2024, which fits 'many such models' and 'very little moat'. Reporting documents a competitive LLM price war in 2024. The packet has no evidence of a lasting lead or of stable prices.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction, listed under 'High confidence'.

semantics.note: A firm 'will' forecast. 'Except possibly in very narrow use cases' is a scope carve-out, not a hedge on the main claim, and the normalised wording keeps it. 'Endlessly' is rhetorical; heavy hype is the testable part.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into hype and general reliability is fair. Treating coding agents as a specialised domain inside the carve-out is a defensible ordinary reading, but the result partly depends on it.

evidence.note: The OpenAI CEO's January 2025 statement is itself an instance of the agent promotion the claim predicted. It is evidence of hype, not of reliability.
Reuters report of Gartner's June 2025 analysis: agent projects mostly driven by hype, widespread 'agent washing', and models lacking the maturity for complex goals.
Independent 2025 benchmark of 175 workplace tasks: the best agent fully completed only 30%.
Karpathy in October 2025 said employee-like agents 'just don't work'. This is expert assessment.
Willison says coding agents worked well in 2025. Under the contract, coding is a specialised domain inside the carve-out, so this does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: Both parts hold for 2025. Agents were heavily promoted, as the CEO statements and Gartner's hype findings show. General-purpose agents remained unreliable: 30% completion on realistic tasks, Gartner's maturity judgement, and Karpathy's assessment. The coding-agent successes fall inside the carve-out as the contract reads it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction, listed under 'High confidence'.

semantics.note: A firm 'will continue' forecast through the end of 2025. The normalised wording is faithful.

contract.note: The plain reading (frequent, material errors documented in 2025; improvement alone does not falsify) is ordinary and fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: Trade-press report of the October 2025 EBU/BBC study of four leading assistants: 45% of answers had a significant issue.
Same study: 20% of answers had major accuracy issues, including hallucinations.
2025 Deloitte incident: AI fabrications in a paid government report led to revision and a partial refund.
The study found some improvement but error levels still high. That does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: Independent 2025 evaluation found high error rates in leading assistants, and a consequential real-world fabrication incident is documented. Improvement was partial and errors stayed material, so the support condition is met. The evidence covers news questions and one incident, not every use.
